children.note: Why water suits life, beyond being a good solvent.
Oxygen pulls electrons from the two hydrogens, giving a bent, polar molecule; each water molecule can hydrogen bond with neighbours.

manas.q: Why is the water molecule polar?

children.note: Evaporating water takes a lot of heat, so sweating is an effective way to lose body heat.

manas.q: Which property of water makes sweating an effective cooling method?

children.note: Water molecules surround dissolved ions and polar groups, orienting their partial charges toward them and keeping them in solution.

manas.q: How does water keep ions in solution?

children.note: Non-polar groups cluster together away from water; this drives lipid bilayer and micelle formation and helps proteins fold.

manas.q: What drives formation of lipid bilayers in water?

children.note: Water dissociates slightly into H+ and OH−; Kw = [H+][OH−] = 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C, so neutral pH is 7 at that temperature.

manas.q: What is the ion product of water at 25 °C?

children.note: Extracellular fluid is mostly interstitial fluid (about three quarters), with plasma making up about one quarter.

manas.q: How is extracellular fluid divided between plasma and interstitial fluid?

children.note: The language of acid–base chemistry.
An acid donates H+; a base accepts H+. Each acid has a conjugate base formed when it loses H+.

manas.q: How does the Brønsted–Lowry theory define acids and bases?

children.note: pH = −log10[H+]. Because the scale is logarithmic, a fall of 1 pH unit means a tenfold rise in [H+].

manas.q: By how much does [H+] change when pH falls by one unit?

children.note: Strong acids dissociate almost completely in water; weak acids only partly, setting up an equilibrium with their conjugate base.

manas.q: What is the difference between strong and weak acids?

children.note: pKa = −log Ka; it is the pH at which an acid is half dissociated, so acid and conjugate base are present in equal amounts.

manas.q: At what pH is a weak acid half dissociated?

children.note: Metabolism makes a large amount of volatile acid as CO2 (cleared by lungs) and a smaller fixed acid load, e.g. sulphuric and phosphoric acids (cleared by kidneys).

manas.q: Which organ clears volatile acid and which clears fixed acid?

children.note: Principles that apply to every buffer.
A mixture of a weak acid and its conjugate base (or weak base and its acid) that limits pH change when acid or alkali is added.

manas.q: What is a buffer?

children.note: The curve is flattest around the pKa, which is where adding acid or base changes pH least.

manas.q: Where on a titration curve is buffering most effective?

children.note: Depends on total buffer concentration and on how close the pKa is to the working pH.

manas.q: What two factors determine buffer capacity?

children.topic: Buffers are only a first line
children.note: Buffers bind H+ within seconds but do not remove acid from the body; lungs and kidneys must finally excrete it.

manas.q: Why can buffers alone not correct an acid load?

children.note: The main extracellular buffer in detail.
CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3−; carbonic anhydrase speeds the first step.

manas.q: Which enzyme speeds the hydration of CO2?

children.note: pH = 6.1 + log([HCO3−] ÷ (0.03 × PCO2 in mmHg)); 0.03 converts PCO2 into dissolved CO2.

manas.q: Write the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for the bicarbonate buffer.

children.note: Normal HCO3− 24 mmol/L and dissolved CO2 1.2 mmol/L give a 20:1 ratio; log 20 ≈ 1.3, and 6.1 + 1.3 = 7.4.

manas.q: What ratio of bicarbonate to dissolved CO2 gives a pH of 7.4?

children.note: Its pKa of 6.1 is far from 7.4, but CO2 is removed by the lungs and HCO3− is set by the kidneys, so the system stays powerful.

manas.q: Why is the bicarbonate buffer effective despite its pKa of 6.1?

children.note: Buffers that matter inside cells and in urine.
H2PO4− ⇌ H+ + HPO4²−, pKa about 6.8; important inside cells and in urine, where it carries titratable acid.

manas.q: What is the approximate pKa of the phosphate buffer?

children.note: Histidine imidazole side chains have a pKa near physiological pH; amino and carboxyl groups also contribute.

manas.q: Which amino acid side chain makes proteins good buffers at body pH?

children.note: Abundant in red cells and rich in histidine; it buffers H+ formed when CO2 enters red cells.

manas.q: Why is haemoglobin an important blood buffer?

children.note: Deoxygenated haemoglobin is a better H+ acceptor than oxyhaemoglobin, so it buffers more acid in the tissues where CO2 is added.

manas.q: Which form of haemoglobin is the better buffer, oxy or deoxy?

children.note: HCO3− made in red cells moves out to plasma in exchange for Cl−, carrying much of the CO2 to the lungs as plasma bicarbonate.

manas.q: What is the chloride shift?

children.note: Tubule cells make NH4+ from glutamine; in the collecting duct NH3 picks up secreted H+ and is trapped as NH4+. Each NH4+ excreted adds a new HCO3− to blood.

manas.q: How does ammonia help the kidney excrete acid?

children.note: The organs that finally set pH.
Chemoreceptors sense rising PCO2 and H+ and increase ventilation, blowing off CO2; this acts within minutes.

manas.q: How quickly does respiratory compensation act?

children.note: In the medulla; CO2 crosses into CSF and lowers its pH, which drives breathing.

manas.q: How do central chemoreceptors detect a rise in arterial CO2?

children.note: Most filtered HCO3− is reclaimed in the proximal tubule via H+ secretion and carbonic anhydrase.

manas.q: Where is most filtered bicarbonate reabsorbed?

children.note: For each H+ excreted as titratable acid or as NH4+, the kidney adds a new HCO3− to blood; this takes hours to days.

manas.q: How does the kidney generate new bicarbonate?

children.note: In the collecting duct, they secrete H+ into urine via an H+-ATPase and return HCO3− to blood.

manas.q: Which collecting duct cells secrete H+?

children.note: Look at the pH first: below 7.35 is acidaemia, above 7.45 alkalaemia.

manas.q: What is the first step in reading an ABG?

children.note: If PCO2 moves in the direction that explains the pH, it is respiratory; if HCO3− does, it is metabolic.

manas.q: How do you decide if an acid–base disorder is respiratory or metabolic?

children.note: No. The other value moves the same way to limit the pH change, but compensation never takes pH past normal (no overcorrection).

manas.q: Does compensation ever return pH past normal?

children.note: Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−); in metabolic acidosis it separates added acids (high gap) from bicarbonate loss (normal gap). Normal range is lab-dependent.

manas.q: How is the anion gap calculated?

children.note: In metabolic acidosis, expected PaCO2 (mmHg) = 1.5 × HCO3− + 8 ± 2; a value outside this suggests a second disorder.

manas.q: What is Winter's formula used for?

children.note: The four primary disorders and common causes.
Low HCO3− from added acid: diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, kidney failure, toxic alcohols, salicylate poisoning.

manas.q: Give causes of high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

children.note: Bicarbonate loss or poor renal acid excretion, e.g. diarrhoea and renal tubular acidosis; chloride rises.

manas.q: Give two causes of normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.

children.note: Raised HCO3−. Vomiting loses gastric HCl, leaving HCO3− behind; volume and chloride loss then make the kidney keep it. Loop and thiazide diuretics also cause it.

manas.q: Why does prolonged vomiting cause metabolic alkalosis?

children.note: Medial means nearer the median plane, lateral farther from it. The thumb is lateral and the little finger medial in the hand.

children.note: Superficial means nearer the body surface; deep means farther from it. The skin is superficial to muscle.

children.note: Abduction raises the arm sideways away from the trunk in the coronal plane; adduction returns it towards the median plane.

manas.q: In which plane is the arm abducted?

children.note: At the ankle, dorsiflexion lifts the top of the foot towards the shin; plantarflexion points the foot and toes down, as on tiptoe.

manas.q: What is dorsiflexion of the foot?

children.note: Turning about an axis and circling.
Rotation turns a bone about its long axis: medial (internal) rotation turns its front towards the midline, lateral (external) away from it.

manas.q: What is medial rotation of a limb?

children.note: A sequence of flexion, abduction, extension and adduction so the distal end traces a circle, e.g. at the shoulder or hip.

manas.q: What is circumduction?

children.note: In pronation the radius rotates around the fixed ulna and crosses over it; in supination the two bones lie parallel again.

manas.q: What happens to the radius during pronation?

children.note: Movements with their own names.
Inversion turns the sole to face medially; eversion turns it laterally. They occur mainly at the subtalar and transverse tarsal joints.

manas.q: At which joints do inversion and eversion mainly occur?

children.note: Moving a part forwards or backwards, e.g. jutting the jaw out or moving the scapula forwards around the chest wall.

manas.q: Give an example of protraction.

children.note: Raising or lowering a part, e.g. shrugging the shoulders (scapular elevation) or opening the mouth (mandibular depression).

manas.q: Give examples of elevation and depression.

children.note: Opposition brings the thumb pad to meet the pad of another digit, mainly at the thumb's carpometacarpal joint; reposition returns it.

manas.q: What is opposition of the thumb?

children.note: Where the usual rules need care.
The thumb lies at right angles to the fingers: its flexion and extension occur in the coronal plane, abduction and adduction in the sagittal plane.

manas.q: In which plane does thumb flexion occur?

children.note: Knee flexion moves the leg posteriorly, the opposite of the elbow, because the lower limb rotates medially during development.

manas.q: Why does the knee flex in the opposite direction to the elbow?

children.note: At the ankle, dorsiflexion and plantarflexion replace flexion and extension because those words are ambiguous there.

manas.q: Why are dorsiflexion and plantarflexion used at the ankle?

children.note: Raising the arm above the head needs rotation of the scapula on the chest wall as well as movement at the shoulder joint itself.

manas.q: Which bone must rotate for full elevation of the arm?

children.note: Where the official words come from.
The international standard list of anatomical terms, in Latin with English equivalents; first published in 1998.

manas.q: What is Terminologia Anatomica?

children.note: Eponyms honour people but say nothing about the structure; e.g. Achilles tendon = calcaneal tendon, Eustachian tube = pharyngotympanic tube.

manas.q: What is the descriptive name for the Achilles tendon?

children.note: Many names describe shape or place: deltoid (triangular), brachium (arm), pollex (thumb), hallux (great toe).

manas.q: What do pollex and hallux mean?

children.note: Supra- means above, infra- below, inter- between, sub- beneath, peri- around.

manas.q: What do the prefixes supra-, infra- and inter- mean?

children.note: Turning terms into clear notes and safe practice.
State the body region, surface and side, the distance from a fixed landmark, then size and depth, so any reader can find it.

manas.q: What details locate a wound precisely in clinical notes?

children.note: Palpable bony points mark deeper structures; the sternal angle lies at the level of the 2nd costal cartilage.

manas.q: Which costal cartilage lies at the level of the sternal angle?

children.note: The common ankle sprain happens in inversion and stretches the lateral ligaments, most often the anterior talofibular ligament.

manas.q: Which ligament is most often injured in an inversion sprain?

children.note: Joint movement is recorded in degrees, starting from the anatomical position taken as zero (neutral-zero method).

manas.q: What is the starting point for measuring joint range?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-20.
Anatomists from FIPAT's gross anatomy group argue TA2 offers several names for one structure, unlike TA1, losing the goal of one agreed international standard.

manas.q: What criticism of TA2 did anatomists raise in 2024?

children.note: AnatomicalTerms.info is a free site linking each Terminologia Anatomica term to synonyms, eponyms and other-language terms, with short open definitions to ease learning.

manas.q: What does the AnatomicalTerms.info site offer students?

children.note: Quick wins.
Supination turns the palm up as if holding a bowl of soup; pronation turns it down.

manas.q: What memory aid helps recall supination?

children.note: Inversion = sole faces in (medially); eversion = sole faces out.

manas.q: Which way does the sole face in inversion?

children.note: Fingers abduct from the middle finger; toes from the second toe.

manas.q: What is the reference line for abduction of the toes?

children.note: In anatomical position the ulna is medial and the radius lateral (thumb side).

manas.q: Which forearm bone is lateral in the anatomical position?

children.note: Remember the rows: hypochondriac–epigastric, lumbar–umbilical, inguinal–hypogastric.

manas.q: List the nine abdominal regions row by row.

maps.title: HMP 100 · In depth: Homeostasis and body fluids

nodeData.topic: Homeostasis and body fluids in depth
nodeData.note: Feedback control, fluid compartments, osmolality, water shifts and basic regulation. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: Keeping the internal environment steady.
Homeostasis is keeping the internal environment (the ECF bathing cells) relatively constant despite outside change; Walter Cannon coined the term.

manas.q: What is homeostasis and who coined the term?

children.note: A sensor detects the variable, a control centre compares it with the set point, and an effector corrects it, linked by afferent and efferent paths.

manas.q: Name the three parts of a homeostatic control system.

children.note: The set point is the value the system defends; the variable swings within a narrow range around it. Set points can reset, e.g. raised in fever.

manas.q: What happens to the temperature set point in fever?

children.note: How control systems respond to change.
A rise in blood pressure stretches baroreceptors, the brainstem cuts sympathetic and boosts vagal output, and heart rate and vessel tone fall.

manas.q: Outline the baroreceptor reflex response to a rise in BP.

children.note: Gain = correction achieved ÷ error that remains; the higher the gain, the more completely the disturbance is corrected.

manas.q: How is the gain of a control system calculated?

children.note: Positive feedback amplifies a change until an outside event stops it, e.g. delivery of the baby ends the oxytocin loop of labour.

manas.q: What ends the positive feedback loop of labour?

children.note: Positive feedback can be deadly: in severe haemorrhage, low pressure starves the heart muscle, the heart weakens and pressure falls further.

manas.q: Give an example of harmful positive feedback.

children.note: An anticipatory response before the variable changes, e.g. saliva and gastric acid secreted at the sight or smell of food.

manas.q: What is feedforward control? Give an example.

children.note: Where body water sits and what divides it.
Fat holds little water, so the fraction of body weight that is water falls with obesity; it is also lower in women and older adults.

manas.q: Why is total body water lower in obese people?

children.note: A small specialised part of ECF in epithelial-lined spaces: CSF, synovial, pleural, peritoneal and intraocular fluid, and gut secretions.

manas.q: Give examples of transcellular fluid.

children.note: About 7% of body weight, roughly 5 L in a 70 kg adult; plasma makes up a little over half of it.

manas.q: What is the normal blood volume of a 70 kg adult?

children.note: The capillary wall separates plasma from interstitial fluid; the cell membrane separates ECF from ICF.

manas.q: What barrier separates plasma from interstitial fluid?

children.note: The indicator-dilution method.
Volume = amount of indicator given (minus any excreted or metabolised) ÷ its concentration once evenly mixed.

manas.q: State the indicator-dilution formula for volume.

children.note: Spreads evenly only within the compartment measured, is not toxic or metabolised, and is easy to measure.

manas.q: List properties of an ideal indicator for volume.

children.note: ICF and interstitial fluid cannot be measured directly: ICF = TBW − ECF; interstitial = ECF − plasma volume.

manas.q: How are ICF and interstitial volumes obtained?

children.note: Blood volume = plasma volume ÷ (1 − haematocrit).

manas.q: How is blood volume calculated from plasma volume?

children.note: Different solutes inside and outside cells.
Chloride and bicarbonate are the main extracellular anions.

manas.q: What are the main anions of ECF?

children.note: Phosphates and proteins are the main intracellular anions; magnesium is an important intracellular cation after potassium.

manas.q: What are the main intracellular anions?

children.note: Ion levels are similar, but plasma has much more protein because capillary walls let little protein through.

manas.q: How does plasma differ from interstitial fluid?

children.note: Free calcium is far lower in the cytosol than in ECF, so calcium entry can act as a signal.

manas.q: Is free calcium higher inside or outside cells?

children.note: In every compartment total positive charges equal total negative charges.

manas.q: What is the principle of electroneutrality?

children.note: How solutes pull water.
Osmolality = osmoles per kg of water; osmolarity = per litre of solution. In dilute body fluids the two are almost the same.

manas.q: What is the difference between osmolality and osmolarity?

children.note: Measured minus calculated osmolality; a raised gap points to unmeasured osmoles such as ethanol, methanol or ethylene glycol.

manas.q: What does a raised osmolal gap suggest?

children.note: Only solutes that cannot cross the membrane move water. Urea crosses cells freely, so it adds to osmolality but not tonicity.

manas.q: Why does urea not contribute to tonicity?

children.note: A solution's effect on cell volume: in isotonic fluid cells keep their size, in hypotonic they swell, in hypertonic they shrink.

manas.q: What happens to red cells in a hypotonic solution?

children.note: 0.9% sodium chloride is about isotonic with plasma, so red cells keep their volume in it.

manas.q: Why is 0.9% sodium chloride called isotonic saline?

children.note: Predicting which compartment changes.
Water crosses cell membranes freely until ICF and ECF osmolality match; sodium stays mainly in the ECF.

manas.q: What determines water movement between ICF and ECF?

children.note: Adding or losing isotonic fluid changes ECF volume only; osmolality is unchanged so no water enters or leaves cells.

manas.q: What happens to ICF volume after isotonic fluid loss?

children.note: Extra water lowers ECF osmolality, water moves into cells, and both compartments expand; cells swell.

manas.q: What happens to cells after a large pure water load?

children.note: Raised ECF osmolality draws water out of cells: ECF expands and ICF shrinks.

manas.q: How does hypertonic saline change ICF and ECF volumes?

children.note: Fluid exchange across capillaries.
Capillary hydrostatic pressure and interstitial oncotic pressure push fluid out; plasma oncotic and interstitial hydrostatic pressure oppose it.

manas.q: Which Starling forces favour filtration out of capillaries?

children.note: Mostly due to albumin; a fall in plasma albumin lets more fluid stay in the tissues.

manas.q: Which plasma protein provides most oncotic pressure?

children.note: Lymph vessels return excess filtered fluid and leaked protein to the blood.

manas.q: What is the role of lymphatics in fluid balance?

children.note: Raised capillary pressure (heart failure), low albumin (nephrotic syndrome, liver disease, kwashiorkor), leaky capillaries (inflammation), blocked lymph (filariasis).

manas.q: List four mechanisms of oedema with examples.

children.note: Intake must match losses.
Drinks, water in food and a small amount of metabolic water from oxidation of nutrients.

manas.q: What are the sources of body water intake?

children.note: Urine (the largest route and the one adjusted to keep water balance), insensible loss from skin and lungs, sweat and faeces.

manas.q: Which route of water loss is adjusted to keep water balance?

children.note: Evaporation from skin and airways that we do not feel; it rises with fever, heat and fast breathing.

manas.q: What increases insensible water loss?

children.note: The basic hormonal controls.
Made in the hypothalamus, released from the posterior pituitary when osmolality rises or volume falls; adds aquaporin-2 channels in collecting ducts.

manas.q: How does ADH increase water reabsorption?

children.note: Driven by raised osmolality, low blood volume and angiotensin II acting on hypothalamic centres.

manas.q: What stimulates thirst?

children.note: Low renal perfusion releases renin; angiotensin II constricts vessels and triggers aldosterone, which makes the kidney retain sodium and water.

manas.q: Outline the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system.

children.note: ANP from atria and BNP from ventricles are released on stretch; they increase sodium and water excretion and oppose RAAS.

manas.q: What do natriuretic peptides do?

children.note: Total body sodium sets ECF volume; water balance sets the sodium concentration.

manas.q: Which controls ECF volume: sodium content or water?

children.note: Applying fluid physiology at the bedside.
Thirst, dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, fast pulse and low urine output.

manas.q: List clinical signs of dehydration.

children.note: Serum sodium below 135 mmol/L, usually too much water for the sodium; brain cells swell, causing confusion or seizures.

manas.q: Why can hyponatraemia cause seizures?

children.note: Serum sodium above 145 mmol/L, usually a water deficit; cells, including brain cells, shrink.

manas.q: What happens to cells in hypernatraemia?

children.note: Isotonic crystalloid spreads through the ECF, so only about a quarter of it stays in the plasma.

manas.q: What fraction of infused isotonic saline stays in plasma?

children.note: The glucose is metabolised, leaving free water that spreads through all body water; little stays in plasma, so it is poor for resuscitation.

manas.q: Why is 5% dextrose poor for restoring blood volume?

children.note: Guidance on IV maintenance fluids in children.
A 2024 viewpoint found international guidelines agree that isotonic fluids are the standard for IV maintenance in ill children.

manas.q: What fluid type do guidelines agree on for paediatric maintenance?

children.note: ESPNIC (European paediatric intensive care) advises isotonic balanced fluid with glucose, restricted volumes in most children, and regular electrolyte and glucose checks.

manas.q: What did ESPNIC 2022 recommend for paediatric IV maintenance?

children.note: Per hour: 4 mL/kg for the first 10 kg, 2 mL/kg for the next 10 kg, 1 mL/kg for each kg above 20. Many guidelines now restrict volumes; follow local guidance.

manas.q: State the Holliday–Segar 4-2-1 rule for maintenance fluid.

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-20.
A systematic review gave 16 recommendations: isotonic balanced fluids providing glucose, restricted volumes for most children, and regular electrolyte, glucose and fluid checks.

manas.q: What were key ESPNIC 2022 maintenance fluid advice points?

children.note: A viewpoint says IV fluids need choice, rate, duration and de-escalation like drugs; most evidence is from rich countries, so fit for LMICs is uncertain.

manas.q: Why did a 2024 viewpoint urge caution applying fluid evidence to LMICs?

children.note: A review notes hospital AKI is common, with risks such as surgery, CKD and heart failure; IV fluid timing, type, amount and rate matter.

manas.q: Which patients are at higher risk of hospital-acquired AKI?

children.note: Quick wins.
TBW ≈ 60% of body weight, ICF ≈ 40%, ECF ≈ 20%.

manas.q: State the 60-40-20 rule.

children.note: 2[Na+] + glucose + urea, all in mmol/L; normal about 285–295 mOsm/kg.

manas.q: Give the formula for calculated plasma osmolality.

children.note: Labour (oxytocin), LH surge, clotting.

manas.q: Name three positive feedback loops.

children.note: ECF: inulin; plasma: Evans blue or labelled albumin; TBW: heavy water.

manas.q: Which marker measures plasma volume?

maps.title: HPS 100 · In depth: Biopsychosocial Model of Health

nodeData.note: Engel's model in depth: roots, three domains, how they interact, clinical use, critiques. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What the model claims and the ideas it grew from.
Health and illness result from biological, psychological and social systems acting on each other at the same time, so all three must be assessed in every patient.

manas.q: What is the core claim of the biopsychosocial model?

children.note: Engel argued in Science (1977) that medicine needed a new model; the biomedical model left no room for the person or their life context.

manas.q: In which journal did Engel set out the biopsychosocial model in 1977?

children.note: Engel drew on systems theory: nature as a hierarchy of linked systems, from cells and organs to the person, family, community and society.

manas.q: Which theory underpins Engel's biopsychosocial model?

children.note: A change at one level (e.g. job loss) can travel up or down the hierarchy and alter others (mood, sleep, blood pressure).

manas.q: How does the hierarchy of systems explain illness in the biopsychosocial model?

children.note: Health is not simply present or absent; people move along a continuum as the three domains shift over time.

manas.q: Is health seen as a yes/no state in the biopsychosocial model?

children.note: The older model the BPS model was built to complete, not to discard.
Explains illness by reducing it to the smallest biological parts, such as cells, molecules or a single pathogen.

manas.q: What is reductionism in the biomedical model?

children.note: Treats mind and body as separate (traced to Descartes), so psychological complaints are seen as outside 'real' medicine.

manas.q: Which philosopher is linked to the mind–body dualism behind the biomedical model?

children.note: Great successes: germ theory, antibiotics, vaccines, surgery. The BPS model keeps biology and adds the person and context.

manas.q: Does the biopsychosocial model reject the biomedical model?

children.note: The biomedical approach puts the doctor as expert and patient as passive; BPS care moves towards shared, patient-centred decisions.

manas.q: How does the role of the patient differ between biomedical and BPS models?

children.note: Typical factors in each domain, used when building a full case formulation.
Genes, age, sex, pathogens, physiology, organ damage, nutrition, drug effects and comorbidities.

manas.q: List examples of biological factors in the BPS model.

children.note: Beliefs, emotions, mood, personality, coping style, cognition, health behaviours and past experiences of illness.

manas.q: List examples of psychological factors in the BPS model.

children.note: Family, social support, income, work, education, housing, culture, religion, stigma and access to services.

manas.q: List examples of social factors in the BPS model.

children.note: The 3 Ps grid crossed with the three domains: what made the person vulnerable, what triggered it, what keeps it going. Some add protective factors.

manas.q: What are the 3 Ps used in a biopsychosocial formulation?

children.note: Pathways that link mind, body and social world.
Perceived stress activates the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis, raising cortisol; chronic activation affects immunity, metabolism and mood.

manas.q: Which hormonal axis links psychological stress to bodily change?

children.note: Acute stress triggers sympathetic activation and adrenaline release: raised heart rate, blood pressure and blood glucose.

manas.q: What does sympathetic activation do during acute stress?

children.note: Study of how mind, nervous, endocrine and immune systems interact; e.g. chronic stress can slow wound healing.

manas.q: What does psychoneuroimmunology study?

children.note: Stress, mood and social setting shape behaviours (smoking, alcohol, diet, exercise, adherence) that then change biology.

manas.q: Give the behavioural pathway by which social factors affect disease.

children.note: Melzack and Wall (1965): spinal 'gates' modulate pain signals, and mood, attention and expectation can open or close them.

manas.q: Who proposed the gate control theory of pain and what does it show?

children.note: Expectation alone can improve (placebo) or worsen (nocebo) symptoms, showing belief has measurable bodily effects.

manas.q: What do placebo and nocebo effects show about mind and body?

children.note: Good social support is linked to better health and is thought to cushion the harmful effects of stress.

manas.q: What is the buffering effect of social support?

children.note: Turning the model into everyday practice.
Beyond symptoms, ask about mood, beliefs, work, family, money, culture and supports, then link them to the problem.

manas.q: What extra areas does a biopsychosocial history cover?

children.note: ICE = Ideas, Concerns, Expectations: asking about these reveals the patient's own view of the illness and helps agree a plan.

manas.q: What does ICE stand for in consultation skills?

children.note: The BPS model underlies patient-centred care: seeing the person, sharing power and building the relationship.

manas.q: Which care approach is built on the biopsychosocial model?

children.note: Doctors, nurses, psychologists, physiotherapists, social workers and community health workers each cover different domains.

manas.q: Why does BPS care often need a multidisciplinary team?

children.note: In back pain, psychosocial 'yellow flags' (fear-avoidance, low mood, poor recovery expectations) are linked to a higher risk of long-term disability.

manas.q: What are yellow flags in low back pain?

children.note: Control depends on biology plus understanding, mood, diet, cost of drugs and family support, not prescriptions alone.

manas.q: Why is the BPS model useful in diabetes care?

children.note: Viral suppression depends on drugs and on stigma, disclosure, food security, transport costs and support groups.

manas.q: How do social factors affect HIV treatment outcomes?

children.note: Depression is common in chronic illness and worsens adherence and outcomes, so screening for mood is part of good care.

manas.q: Why screen for depression in chronic physical illness?

children.note: Many Kenyans use traditional or faith healing alongside clinics; asking respectfully about this is part of the social domain.

manas.q: Why ask Kenyan patients about traditional or faith healing?

children.note: Why some call the model vague, and how it has been extended.
Critics say it lists factors without saying how they combine or which matters most for a given patient.

manas.q: What is the main theoretical criticism of the biopsychosocial model?

children.note: Wrongly blaming symptoms on stress can delay diagnosis of physical disease; biology must still be investigated properly.

manas.q: What is the danger of over-applying the psychological domain?

children.note: Full BPS assessment takes time, training and team support that busy clinics may lack.

manas.q: Name a practical barrier to using the BPS model.

children.note: Some add a spiritual domain (bio-psycho-social-spiritual), important in palliative care and in many Kenyan communities.

manas.q: What fourth domain do some add to the BPS model?

children.note: How the model shows up in global frameworks.
The International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health uses a biopsychosocial approach: body, activity, participation and context.

manas.q: Which WHO classification uses a biopsychosocial approach to disability?

children.note: The medical model locates disability in the body; the social model in barriers in society. The ICF combines both.

manas.q: How does the ICF combine the medical and social models of disability?

children.note: WHO's Mental Health Gap Action Programme supports non-specialists in primary care to manage common mental disorders.

manas.q: What is the aim of WHO's mhGAP programme?

children.note: WHO health promotion charter: health is created and lived by people in the settings of everyday life, shaped by social conditions, so action goes beyond the health sector.

manas.q: What did the Ottawa Charter say about where health is created?

children.note: UK and other national guidelines advise assessing psychosocial factors and favour exercise and self-management over imaging for most low back pain.

manas.q: What do major low back pain guidelines advise beyond biology?

children.note: Recent papers on the model, from Europe PMC.
Authors propose rebuilding the model on general scientific theories (causation as regulation, dysfunction as dysregulation), citing psychotherapy and social epidemiology findings as support.

manas.q: What core idea does the 2023 'revitalized' BPS model use for dysfunction?

children.note: A narrative review in musculoskeletal pain finds the model is often used narrowly or reductively, in two parallel versions, 'humanistic' and 'causation'; an 'enactive' approach could unite them.

manas.q: What two versions of the BPS model did the 2023 review describe?

children.note: An umbrella review linked worse long-term outcome in acute–subacute back pain to high pain and disability, distress, negative expectations and heavy physical work.

manas.q: Which factors were linked to poor outcome in acute low back pain in the 2022 umbrella review?
manas.ref: Int J Environ Res Public Health 2022

children.note: Quick points examiners like.
For any case, draw a 3×3 grid: predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating against bio, psycho, social.

manas.q: How would you structure a biopsychosocial formulation in an exam?

children.note: Always state the model adds to, rather than replaces, biomedical diagnosis and treatment.

manas.q: Does the BPS model replace biomedical treatment?

children.note: Strong answers cite a pathway: HPA axis, gate control, behaviour, or social support buffering.

manas.q: Name two mechanisms that link psychological stress to disease.

children.note: Illustrate with HIV, diabetes or TB care where cost, stigma and support shape outcomes.

manas.q: Give a Kenyan example showing all three BPS domains.
